title: Benchmarking and Profiling Without Lying to Yourself

questions.question: A loop times HashMap.get and then TreeMap.get, once each, in a fresh JVM, and reports TreeMap as 9x faster. Which explanation is most likely?
options: TreeMap.get really is faster for integer keys because comparisons are cheaper than hashing
The HashMap loop ran while the JVM was still interpreting bytecode, before the JIT compiled the lookup
HashMap.get allocates on every call and the garbage collector ran during its loop
Sequential integer keys collide in a HashMap and degrade every lookup to a linear scan
questions.explanation: The first code to run in a JVM is interpreted; C1 and C2 compile it only after thousands of invocations, so whichever loop runs first pays the warm-up cost. HashMap.get does not allocate, Integer hashing does not collide for sequential keys, and TreeMap.get is O(log n) pointer chasing, which is slower once both are compiled.

questions.question: Using nearest-rank percentiles on the ten sorted samples 10, 20, ..., 100, what are p50 and p99?
options: 55 and 99.1, interpolating between the neighbouring samples
50 and 100: ranks ceil(0.5 * 10) = 5 and ceil(0.99 * 10) = 10
60 and 100: the median rounds up and p99 is the maximum
50 and 90: p99 excludes the single largest sample as an outlier
questions.explanation: Nearest rank picks the sample at 1-based rank ceil(p/100 * n): rank 5 is 50 and rank 10 is 100. It never interpolates, so every reported percentile is a value that occurred. Excluding the largest sample would hide exactly the tail event p99 exists to show.

questions.question: A benchmark row reports per-fork medians [60, 8, 8] and a pooled p50 of 11 ns. What should you conclude?
options: The operation costs 11 ns; the pooled median is the most robust single number
The operation costs about 25 ns, the mean of the three fork medians
The forks disagree because the first was still compiling; the row is unstable and should not be quoted
The second and third forks were cached by the CPU, so 60 ns is the honest cold figure
questions.explanation: A 7x disagreement between forks means the runs did not measure the same thing: the first fork paid for JIT compilation of the harness loop. The harness marks it UNSTABLE for this reason. Neither the pooled median nor the mean of the medians is a measurement of the operation; the fix is more warm-up or real forks.

questions.question: Why does every benchmark body hand its result to a Blackhole whose consume writes a volatile field?
options: To warm the memory subsystem so that the first measured iteration is not a cold-cache outlier
Because a computation whose result has no observable effect may be deleted by the JIT, leaving an empty loop
To force a garbage collection between iterations so GC pauses land outside the timed region
Because System.nanoTime is only accurate when a memory barrier separates consecutive reads
questions.explanation: Dead-code elimination removes work whose result nobody reads. A volatile write is a side effect the compiler must preserve, so the computation feeding it survives. The blackhole has nothing to do with caches, GC timing, or nanoTime accuracy.

questions.question: A closed-loop generator intends one request per millisecond. It records 999 latencies of 0.2 ms and one of 2,000 ms. After the coordinated-omission correction, roughly what is p99?
options: Still about 0.2 ms; the correction only changes the maximum
About 20 ms; the stall is spread evenly over the 999 other samples
About 1,000 ms; the correction adds one sample at half the stall duration
About 1,970 ms; 1,999 back-filled samples from 1 ms to 1,999 ms push rank 2,970 deep into the stall
questions.explanation: During a 2 s stall the generator should have sent 1,999 more requests, waiting 1,999 ms, 1,998 ms, ..., 1 ms. With 2,999 samples, p99 is rank ceil(0.99 * 2999) = 2970, which is the 1,971st back-filled value: 1,971 ms. Raw p99 was 0.2 ms, which is the lie coordinated omission tells.

questions.question: A sampling profile shows computeFees with 0% self time and 70% inclusive time, and Money.times with 60% self and 60% inclusive. What does this tell you?
options: computeFees is idle and can be deleted outright; Money.times is the only method in the program doing any work
The profiler suffers from safepoint bias and has attributed computeFees's own loop time to the callee it inlined
Money.times is the hot leaf; computeFees is never the leaf but 70% of samples are beneath it, so calling it less is the structural fix
The two figures contradict each other, because a frame's inclusive time can never exceed the self time of its largest callee
questions.explanation: Self time is samples where the frame was executing; inclusive is samples where it was anywhere on the stack. computeFees spends all its time in callees (Money.times at 60% and another 10%), so it is the frame to restructure, while Money.times is the one to micro-optimise. Inclusive can exceed one callee's self time because it sums over all callees.
